projects.title: Mapping across ground & air.
projects.summary: I’m building a 3D mapping system around two views of the same place: one from a rover and one from a drone.

sections.title: Two views of the same place
sections.body: A rover sees the ground up close. A drone can see over the things that block the rover’s view. I want to find out whether those two perspectives can fill in each other’s gaps.

sections.title: Getting the maps to agree
sections.body: Each platform has its own estimate of where it is. If either estimate drifts, the same wall could end up in two places when the maps are combined. My first milestone is to get a small area that both platforms have seen to line up in one coordinate frame.

projects.title: Air hockey against a robot
projects.summary: Our ME 360 brief called for at least 2.5 degrees of freedom. We built an air-hockey opponent that slides in X and Y and spins a mallet.
projects.technical: MATLAB sends G-code over serial. The controller acknowledges queued commands, and M400 waits for the moves to finish. X and Y use position commands, while the rotary motor runs at a set PWM power. The 3D assembly combines original part exports with approximate frame and drive geometry reconstructed from the video.

gallery.caption: The completed ENG ME 360 game in play.

sections.title: We made a game out of the brief
sections.body: We cut goals into the table and gave the player two ways to shoot: flick the puck like in carrom or hit it with a handheld mallet. On the other side, the robot moves its own mallet around the table. We randomized its motion so a player couldn’t count on the same opening every time.

sections.title: The first demo moved one axis at a time
sections.body: Our sequential demo moved the bridge, moved the carriage, then spun the mallet. It was a good way to check each motion on its own. For the game, we kept the mallet spinning and queued several side-to-side moves at randomized distances before bringing the carriage back to center.

sections.title: Two motors, one bridge
sections.body: The bridge is belt-driven on both sides. MATLAB sends both motors the same travel in opposite motor directions so the two ends advance together. We had to start with the bridge square and set zero by hand. The controller can finish every move it’s given and still be off if the physical starting point is wrong.

sections.title: What we got working
sections.body: The video shows the finished game in play. Getting there meant treating the motion sequence as part of the game design. The same hardware could run through a tidy checklist of moves or give the player a moving target they had to watch.

projects.title: Drawing with two axes
projects.summary: In class, we used two motorized stages and a pen to draw a geometric outline on paper.
projects.tools: Linear stages / lead screws / pen carriage

sections.title: The pen shows what both axes did
sections.body: One lead-screw stage moves the crossbar, and the other moves the pen along it. A line on the page is a record of their combined motion. The corners make that especially easy to see because the pen has to change direction at a specific point.

sections.title: From four corners to a path
sections.body: The class video shows the hardware drawing. I’ve included a small MATLAB simulation alongside it to show the path math. Give it the corners of a rectangle and it fills in points along each edge, including the move back to the start. The simulation was made after class and runs on screen.

projects.title: A robotic arm that stamps paper
projects.summary: The arm had a four-step job: pick a stamp from the rack, ink it, press it onto paper, then put it back.

gallery.caption: Overhead controller view with the rack, ink pad, paper, and return step labeled.
Side view of the arm linkage and curved stamp rack.
Side view of the arm demonstration.

sections.title: The layout was part of the mechanism
sections.body: The rack, ink pad, and paper all had to sit within reach of the same arm. The rack curves around the base, and the controller view lays out the stops in order. Reaching a slot is only half the job. The arm also needs enough room to lift the stamp clear and carry it to the next station.

sections.title: Following the stamp
sections.body: The overhead controller view is where I’d start. It shows the whole job in one frame, with the stations labeled and the arm’s joint angles visible. The other views show how the linkage folds as the end of the arm moves in and out.

projects.title: InsideFPV.
projects.summary: I built drones and oversaw three projects as a CAD intern at InsideFPV.
projects.modelNote: Exterior study reconstructed from a product image.

sections.title: From CAD to the bench
sections.body: I worked on both sides of the build, drawing parts in CAD and assembling drones. At the bench, fit has a second meaning. A part can fit in the model and still be awkward to install if there’s no room to get a tool in or route a wire.

projects.title: Deskinator.
projects.summary: I went from a dimensioned sketch to a wheeled prototype for vacuuming crumbs off a desk.

gallery.caption: Bench prototype with the wiring and drive wheels exposed.
Electronics and motors laid out during assembly.
Dimensioned sketch showing the vacuum, dirt compartment, battery, and wheel positions.

sections.title: Where does the dirt go?
sections.body: The vacuum needed a path for the crumbs and somewhere to collect them. I sketched the intake and dirt compartment, then had to find room for the battery and drive wheels in the same footprint. The top, side, and front views show how much of the design came down to fitting everything together.

sections.title: The sketch and the build
sections.body: In the bench photos, you can see the wheels, wiring, and electronics sharing space with the cleaning hardware. If I built it again, I’d test the intake on its own first and see what it actually picks up before building the rest of the chassis around it.

projects.title: 4-bar linkage.
projects.summary: I used a SolidWorks motion study to see how the links and pivots move together through a cycle.

gallery.caption: SolidWorks assembly with the motion-study timeline open.

sections.title: The position between the screenshots
sections.body: A linkage can look fine in one pose. I wanted to see what happened as it moved through the rest of its travel, so I used the motion timeline to step through the assembly.

sections.title: What I’d check on a physical build
sections.body: I’d start where the links come closest to the frame. The CAD gives me a path to check. The real clearance would also depend on the fasteners, spacers, and any play in the joints.

projects.title: Innovic / FANUC
projects.summary: At Innovic, I programmed and set up a FANUC robot, designed precision fixtures, and helped get parts fabricated across shifts.

gallery.caption: FANUC tool head near the workpiece.
The FANUC arm on the shop floor.

sections.title: Where the part sits matters
sections.body: I worked on both the robot setup and the jigs and fixtures for a precision fabrication job. The fixture locates the workpiece in the real world. If the next part sits differently, the robot can run the same path and still end up in the wrong place relative to the part.

sections.title: Handing the job over
sections.body: I helped take parts from CAD to fabrication and coordinate the work across production shifts. The fixture was the part of the setup that could carry a locating decision from one shift to the next.

projects.title: How a robot figures out where it is
projects.summary: My 2023 research looked at how sensor fusion and algorithm choices affect localization in SLAM.

sections.title: A bad position estimate shows up in the map
sections.body: In simultaneous localization and mapping, the robot builds a map while estimating its own position. If that estimate drifts, it can put a wall in the wrong place. My research asked how combining sensor readings and changing the algorithm could help keep the position estimate on track.

sections.title: How much work should the robot do?
sections.body: Adding observations can help constrain where the robot is, but processing them also takes time. I looked at accuracy and computation together because a moving robot or UAV has to keep updating its position as it goes.
